concepts.title: Case Study: Belgium - Accommodation through Power-sharing

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Case Study: Belgium - Accommodation through Power-sharing' refers to.
questions.a: Belgium is a small European country with a complex ethnic composition: 59% live in the Flemish region and speak Dutch, 40% live in the Wallonia region and speak French, and 1% speak German. The Belgian government adopted an accommodation policy through power-sharing to manage tensions between the Dutch-speaking and French-speaking communities.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Case Study: Belgium - Accommodation through Power-sharing'.
questions.a: Belgium resolved ethnic conflict by sharing power among communities through a constitution that prescribed equal representation and special arrangements.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Case Study: Belgium - Accommodation through Power-sharing' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Case Study: Belgium

concepts.title: Case Study: Sri Lanka - Majoritarianism and its Consequences

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Case Study: Sri Lanka - Majoritarianism and its Consequences' refers to.
questions.a: Sri Lanka is an island nation with diverse population groups: Sinhala speakers (74%), Tamil speakers (18%) including Sri Lankan Tamils (13%) and Indian Tamils, and about 7% Christians who use both Sinhala and Tamil. The Sinhala majority government adopted majoritarian policies that discriminated against Tamils, leading to a civil war.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Case Study: Sri Lanka - Majoritarianism and its Consequences'.
questions.a: Sri Lanka's majoritarian policies favoured the Sinhala majority and marginalised the Tamil minority, ultimately resulting in a violent civil war.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Case Study: Sri Lanka - Majoritarianism and its Consequences' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Case Study: Sri Lanka

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Forms of Power-sharing: Horizontal Distribution' refers to.
questions.a: Horizontal distribution of power involves sharing power among different organs of government at the same level, such as the legislature, executive, and judiciary. This is also called horizontal power-sharing or a system of checks and balances.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Forms of Power-sharing: Horizontal Distribution'.
questions.a: Horizontal power-sharing ensures that no single organ of government exercises unlimited power; each organ checks the others.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Forms of Power-sharing: Horizontal Distribution' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Forms of Power-sharing

concepts.title: Forms of Power-sharing: Vertical Distribution (Federal Division)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Forms of Power-sharing: Vertical Distribution (Federal Division)' refers to.
questions.a: Vertical division of power involves sharing power among governments at different levels: a general government for the entire country (central/national government) and governments at the provincial or regional level (state governments). This is the federal division of power.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Forms of Power-sharing: Vertical Distribution (Federal Division)'.
questions.a: Vertical power-sharing distributes authority between the central government and lower-level governments, allowing each to govern in its own jurisdiction.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Forms of Power-sharing: Vertical Distribution (Federal Division)' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Forms of Power-sharing

concepts.title: Forms of Power-sharing: Among Social Groups

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Forms of Power-sharing: Among Social Groups' refers to.
questions.a: Power-sharing among social groups involves sharing power with minority or marginalised communities, such as religious and linguistic groups. This may take the form of community governments or reserved constituencies in legislatures to give these groups a fair share of power.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Forms of Power-sharing: Among Social Groups'.
questions.a: Sharing power with minority and marginalised groups ensures their voices are heard and protects their interests in a diverse society.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Forms of Power-sharing: Among Social Groups' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Forms of Power-sharing

concepts.title: Forms of Power-sharing: Among Political Parties and Pressure Groups

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Forms of Power-sharing: Among Political Parties and Pressure Groups' refers to.
questions.a: Power-sharing among political parties and pressure groups occurs when different parties compete in elections and share power, either through coalition governments or as opposition. Pressure groups and interest groups also share governmental power through participation in committees or by influencing decision-making.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Forms of Power-sharing: Among Political Parties and Pressure Groups'.
questions.a: In a democracy, power is shared among political parties through competition and coalition, and pressure groups influence decisions to represent specific interests.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Forms of Power-sharing: Among Political Parties and Pressure Groups' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Forms of Power-sharing

concepts.title: Need for Power-sharing: Prudential and Moral Reasons

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Need for Power-sharing: Prudential and Moral Reasons' refers to.
questions.a: Power-sharing is desirable for two sets of reasons. Prudential reasons are based on calculation of gains and losses - sharing power helps reduce conflict and maintain stability. Moral reasons emphasise the intrinsic worth of power-sharing as it is the very spirit of democracy: people have a right to be consulted on how they are governed.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Need for Power-sharing: Prudential and Moral Reasons'.
questions.a: Power-sharing is justified by prudential reasons (stability and conflict reduction) and moral reasons (democratic rights and legitimacy).

questions.q: Under which section is 'Need for Power-sharing: Prudential and Moral Reasons' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Why Power-sharing is Desirable

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Power-sharing in India' refers to.
questions.a: India practises power-sharing through multiple forms: vertical division between the central and state governments, horizontal distribution among the legislature, executive, and judiciary, sharing among social groups through reserved constituencies, and sharing among political parties through elections and coalitions.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Power-sharing in India'.
questions.a: India combines all major forms of power-sharing - horizontal, vertical, among social groups, and among political parties - to manage its vast diversity.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Power-sharing in India' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Power-sharing in India
